CYTOGENETICS LABORATORY REPORT
[redacted location] Medical Center
Department of Clinical Genetics

PATIENT INFORMATION
Patient Name: [redacted name]
Date of Birth: [redacted date]
Medical Record Number: [redacted ID]
Specimen Type: Cord blood
Date Collected: [redacted date]
Date Received: [redacted date]
Date Reported: [redacted date]

CLINICAL INDICATION
Abnormal prenatal ultrasound demonstrating congenital heart defect. Karyotype analysis requested to evaluate for chromosomal abnormalities.

TEST PERFORMED
High-resolution G-banded karyotype analysis
Methodology: Cultured cord blood lymphocytes were harvested and G-banded using trypsin-Giemsa staining. Analysis performed at >550 band resolution.

RESULT
Karyotype: 46,XY,del(4)(p16.3)

ABNORMAL MALE KARYOTYPE

DETAILED FINDINGS
Chromosome analysis revealed a male karyotype with 46 chromosomes. A terminal deletion of the short arm of chromosome 4 at band p16.3 was identified in all 20 metaphases examined. The deletion breakpoint appears to be within band 4p16.3, with loss of all distal chromosomal material.

Band-level analysis:
- Breakpoint: 4p16.3
- Deleted region: 4p16.3→4pter
- All other chromosomes appear structurally normal
- No evidence of mosaicism detected

INTERPRETATION
The terminal deletion of chromosome 4p16.3 identified in this fetus is consistent with Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome (WHS, OMIM #194190). This chromosomal abnormality involves loss of the critical region at 4p16.3, which includes the WHSC1 and WHSC2 genes among others.

Clinical features associated with Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome include:
- Prenatal and postnatal growth restriction
- Intellectual disability (typically severe)
- Characteristic facial features ("Greek warrior helmet" appearance)
- Congenital heart defects (present in ~50% of cases)
- Seizures (>90% of cases)
- Skeletal abnormalities
- Genitourinary anomalies

The congenital heart defect identified on prenatal ultrasound is consistent with the Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome phenotype. Common cardiac manifestations include atrial septal defects, ventricular septal defects, and pulmonary stenosis.

Prognosis depends on the size of the deletion and associated malformations. Mortality is highest in the first two years of life, primarily related to cardiac complications and respiratory infections.

RECOMMENDATIONS
1. Genetic counseling to discuss diagnosis, prognosis, and recurrence risk
2. Parental karyotype analysis recommended to determine if the deletion is de novo or inherited from a balanced translocation carrier parent
3. If pregnancy continues:
   - Referral to pediatric cardiology for comprehensive cardiac evaluation and management planning
   - Referral to pediatric neurology for seizure risk assessment and management
   - Multidisciplinary team coordination including developmental pediatrics
   - Early intervention services planning
4. Prenatal diagnosis available for future pregnancies

TEST LIMITATIONS
This analysis was performed at >550 band resolution. Smaller deletions, duplications, or rearrangements below this resolution may not be detected. This test does not detect point mutations, methylation abnormalities, or low-level mosaicism (<10%).

Laboratory Director: [redacted name], MD, PhD
